title: CSCE 469 Midterm Practice: Cybersecurity Core Concepts
description: Comprehensive practice questions based on CSCE 469 cybersecurity slides 03-07, 11, and 12. Excludes introductions, project proposals, and Android-focused decks. Explanations include deck and slide references for review.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the course definition of security?

choices.label: A condition of freedom from risk or danger, never absolute
choices.value: A condition of freedom from risk or danger, never absolute

choices.label: A collection of hardware, software, policies, and procedures
choices.value: A collection of hardware, software, policies, and procedures

choices.label: A guarantee that no incident will occur
choices.value: A guarantee that no incident will occur

questions.correctAnswer: A condition of freedom from risk or danger, never absolute
questions.explanation: Security is a condition, not a product list, and risk can be eliminated, reduced, or tolerated. Source: Deck 03, slide 7.

questions.prompt: Which are the three elements of the CIA triad?
questions.correctAnswer: availability,confidentiality,integrity
questions.explanation: CIA means confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Accountability is important but is not one of the three CIA terms. Source: Deck 03, slide 8.

questions.prompt: A payroll record is changed by an unauthorized person. Which CIA property was violated most directly?
questions.correctAnswer: Integrity
questions.explanation: Integrity guards against improper modification or destruction of information. Source: Deck 03, slide 8.

questions.prompt: Complete the course risk relationship: risk = threat × _____.
questions.correctAnswer: impact
questions.explanation: The slide defines risk as threat times the consequence to the targeted assets, namely impact. Source: Deck 03, slide 18.

questions.prompt: Which option correctly distinguishes a vulnerability from an exploit?

choices.label: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a method that takes advantage of it
choices.value: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a method that takes advantage of it

choices.label: A vulnerability is an attack; an exploit is the damaged asset
choices.value: A vulnerability is an attack; an exploit is the damaged asset

choices.label: A vulnerability is the impact; an exploit is the probability of attack
choices.value: A vulnerability is the impact; an exploit is the probability of attack

questions.correctAnswer: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is a method that takes advantage of it
questions.explanation: A vulnerability is a flaw in protections; an exploit is the method used to take advantage of that flaw. Source: Deck 03, slide 18.

questions.prompt: After identifying and assessing risk, which responses does the deck list?
questions.correctAnswer: accept,avoid,mitigate,transfer
questions.explanation: The listed responses are avoid, transfer, mitigate, and accept/manage residual risk. Insurance may be bought for residual risk but is not a replacement for those decisions. Source: Deck 03, slide 22.

questions.prompt: Which is the best example of a transfer of risk in the slides?

choices.label: Outsourcing payment-card transactions to a third party
choices.value: Outsourcing payment-card transactions to a third party

questions.correctAnswer: Outsourcing payment-card transactions to a third party
questions.explanation: The deck uses outsourcing payment-card transactions as an example of transferring some risk to a third party. Source: Deck 03, slide 22.

questions.prompt: In the functional security requirements, which term means entities cannot repudiate their actions?
questions.correctAnswer: Accountability
questions.explanation: Accountability requires entities to be fully accountable for, and unable to repudiate, their actions. Source: Deck 03, slide 25.

questions.prompt: What is a central Zero Trust assumption?

choices.label: No implicit trust is granted solely because of network location or asset ownership
choices.value: No implicit trust is granted solely because of network location or asset ownership

choices.label: Internal-network users are trusted by default
choices.value: Internal-network users are trusted by default

choices.label: A perimeter firewall makes further authorization unnecessary
choices.value: A perimeter firewall makes further authorization unnecessary

questions.correctAnswer: No implicit trust is granted solely because of network location or asset ownership
questions.explanation: Zero Trust shifts focus from a static perimeter to users, assets, and resources and rejects location-based implicit trust. Source: Deck 03, slide 29.

questions.prompt: What principle grants an entity only the minimum system resources and authorizations needed to perform its function?
questions.correctAnswer: least privilege
questions.explanation: Least privilege restricts users or processes to the minimum necessary authorizations and resources. Source: Deck 03, slide 34.

questions.prompt: Which configuration reflects secure defaults?

choices.label: Require password changes and make unnecessary features or open ports opt-in
choices.value: Require password changes and make unnecessary features or open ports opt-in

choices.label: Ship default credentials for administrator convenience
choices.value: Ship default credentials for administrator convenience

choices.label: Enable all services so users can choose later
choices.value: Enable all services so users can choose later

choices.label: Hide the default password in documentation
choices.value: Hide the default password in documentation

questions.correctAnswer: Require password changes and make unnecessary features or open ports opt-in
questions.explanation: Secure defaults avoid exploitable default credentials and require explicit opt-in for unnecessary features and services. Source: Deck 03, slide 36.

questions.prompt: What does defense in depth mean?

choices.label: Use multiple, layered countermeasures so one missed attack may be caught by another
choices.value: Use multiple, layered countermeasures so one missed attack may be caught by another

choices.label: Rely on one exceptionally strong control
choices.value: Rely on one exceptionally strong control

choices.label: Hide implementation details as the only control
choices.value: Hide implementation details as the only control

choices.label: Put every service on one trusted network
choices.value: Put every service on one trusted network

questions.correctAnswer: Use multiple, layered countermeasures so one missed attack may be caught by another
questions.explanation: Defense in depth layers heterogeneous countermeasures across attack vectors and includes people, technology, and operations. Source: Deck 03, slide 38.

questions.prompt: Which statement about compliance is correct according to the slides?

choices.label: Being compliant does not necessarily mean being secure
choices.value: Being compliant does not necessarily mean being secure

choices.label: Compliance applies only to physical security
choices.value: Compliance applies only to physical security

questions.correctAnswer: Being compliant does not necessarily mean being secure
questions.explanation: Laws and regulations can lag threats, so compliance is not equivalent to security. Source: Deck 03, slide 45.

questions.prompt: What is the first rule of cryptography in the slides?

choices.label: Never develop or use your own cryptography
choices.value: Never develop or use your own cryptography

choices.label: Encrypt every message with a public key
choices.value: Encrypt every message with a public key

questions.correctAnswer: Never develop or use your own cryptography
questions.explanation: The deck emphasizes using evaluated modules, standard algorithms, and appropriate secure protocols instead of home-grown cryptography. Source: Deck 04, slide 3.

questions.prompt: What term names the original readable message before encryption?
questions.correctAnswer: plaintext
questions.explanation: A message before encryption is plaintext, also called cleartext. Source: Deck 04, slide 5.

questions.prompt: Which statement follows Kerckhoffs-style guidance in the deck?

choices.label: The algorithm should be open, published, and available; keys provide secrecy
choices.value: The algorithm should be open, published, and available; keys provide secrecy

choices.label: The algorithm must be secret but keys may be public
choices.value: The algorithm must be secret but keys may be public

choices.label: Both algorithm and key must be secret
choices.value: Both algorithm and key must be secret

choices.label: No key is needed if the algorithm is unpublished
choices.value: No key is needed if the algorithm is unpublished

questions.correctAnswer: The algorithm should be open, published, and available; keys provide secrecy
questions.explanation: Modern ciphers use keys; their algorithms should be open, published, and broadly available. Source: Deck 04, slide 9.

questions.prompt: An attacker has intercepted ciphertext only and attempts to recover plaintext or deduce a key. What attack class is this?
questions.correctAnswer: Ciphertext-only
questions.explanation: Ciphertext-only cryptanalysis begins with intercepted ciphertext and aims to recover plaintexts or deduce keys. Source: Deck 04, slide 10.

questions.prompt: Which is the deck’s sole example of unconditional security when properly generated, distributed, and used?
questions.correctAnswer: One-time pad
questions.explanation: The slides identify the properly used one-time pad as the only example of unconditional security. Source: Deck 04, slide 11.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a cryptographic hash?

choices.label: Produce a fixed-length output from an arbitrary-length input
choices.value: Produce a fixed-length output from an arbitrary-length input

choices.label: Recover an input exactly from a digest
choices.value: Recover an input exactly from a digest

choices.label: Encrypt a message with a shared secret
choices.value: Encrypt a message with a shared secret

choices.label: Hide a message inside an image
choices.value: Hide a message inside an image

questions.correctAnswer: Produce a fixed-length output from an arbitrary-length input
questions.explanation: A one-way hash maps arbitrary-length pre-images to a fixed-length numeric output and should make collisions hard to generate. Source: Deck 04, slide 17.

questions.prompt: Which property does a MAC provide according to the slides?

choices.label: Message integrity and sender authentication, not confidentiality
choices.value: Message integrity and sender authentication, not confidentiality

questions.correctAnswer: Message integrity and sender authentication, not confidentiality
questions.explanation: The MAC slide explicitly says this is message integrity and authentication, not message confidentiality. Source: Deck 04, slide 18.

questions.prompt: Why do practical hybrid cryptosystems use asymmetric cryptography primarily for session keys?

choices.label: Asymmetric cryptography is much slower, so symmetric crypto protects message traffic
choices.value: Asymmetric cryptography is much slower, so symmetric crypto protects message traffic

questions.correctAnswer: Asymmetric cryptography is much slower, so symmetric crypto protects message traffic
questions.explanation: Asymmetric crypto is roughly three orders of magnitude slower and is used to protect/distribute session keys; symmetric crypto protects traffic. Source: Deck 04, slide 23.

questions.prompt: A public-key digital signature can provide which properties?
questions.correctAnswer: authentication,integrity,nonrepudiation
questions.explanation: Public-key signatures provide origin authentication, integrity, and inability to repudiate. Signing alone does not provide confidentiality. Source: Deck 04, slide 28.

questions.prompt: In a PKI, what does a certification authority do to make public keys trustworthy?

choices.label: Signs public keys or certificates so recipients can verify their integrity and binding
choices.value: Signs public keys or certificates so recipients can verify their integrity and binding

choices.label: Encrypts all application data with one global key
choices.value: Encrypts all application data with one global key

questions.correctAnswer: Signs public keys or certificates so recipients can verify their integrity and binding
questions.explanation: A trusted authority signs public keys and participants verify its signature; practical systems bind keys and identity information in certificates. Source: Deck 04, slide 34.

questions.prompt: Why is a password salt stored with the password hash?

choices.label: It makes dictionary attacks more expensive by varying the input to the public hash
choices.value: It makes dictionary attacks more expensive by varying the input to the public hash

choices.label: It lets the server decrypt the password
choices.value: It lets the server decrypt the password

choices.label: It makes the hash algorithm secret
choices.value: It makes the hash algorithm secret

choices.label: It replaces the need for a password
choices.value: It replaces the need for a password

questions.correctAnswer: It makes dictionary attacks more expensive by varying the input to the public hash
questions.explanation: A random salt is appended before hashing and stored with the resulting hash, increasing the cost of dictionary attacks. Source: Deck 04, slide 44.

questions.prompt: What is a principal advantage of ECC cited in the deck?

choices.label: Equivalent strength with much smaller keys, helpful for less powerful IoT devices
choices.value: Equivalent strength with much smaller keys, helpful for less powerful IoT devices

questions.correctAnswer: Equivalent strength with much smaller keys, helpful for less powerful IoT devices
questions.explanation: ECC can deliver equivalent strength with smaller keys, making it faster and suitable for lower-power devices. Source: Deck 04, slide 45.

questions.prompt: KMIP identifies which three primary elements?
questions.correctAnswer: attributes,objects,operations
questions.explanation: KMIP covers cryptographic objects, actions performed on those objects, and object properties/attributes. Source: Deck 04, slide 46.

questions.prompt: Which technology counters a man-in-the-middle key-exchange attack described in the deck?

choices.label: Verify digitally signed public-key certificates from a trusted KDC/CA
choices.value: Verify digitally signed public-key certificates from a trusted KDC/CA

choices.label: Use only a longer plaintext message
choices.value: Use only a longer plaintext message

questions.correctAnswer: Verify digitally signed public-key certificates from a trusted KDC/CA
questions.explanation: Digital signatures by the KDC/CA let Alice and Bob validate the public keys/certificates and counter the key substitution underlying the attack. Source: Deck 04, slide 43.

questions.prompt: Why is security different from many other software quality attributes?

choices.label: The complete set of possible vulnerabilities is generally unknown
choices.value: The complete set of possible vulnerabilities is generally unknown

questions.correctAnswer: The complete set of possible vulnerabilities is generally unknown
questions.explanation: Many quality attributes have finite known properties to check; assessing security must contend with an unknown set of possible vulnerabilities. Source: Deck 05, slide 7.

questions.prompt: Which analysis verifies properties by examining implementation logic without executing the software?
questions.correctAnswer: Static program analysis
questions.explanation: Static analysis examines implementation logic without executing the system. Source: Deck 05, slide 9.

questions.prompt: Which approach verifies properties through execution and runtime data collection?
questions.correctAnswer: Dynamic program analysis
questions.explanation: Dynamic program analysis relies on execution and collection of runtime data. Source: Deck 05, slide 10.

questions.prompt: Which approach can provide certain guarantees through mathematically sound and complete methods?
questions.correctAnswer: Formal verification
questions.explanation: Formal verification uses mathematically sound and complete methods that can provide certain guarantees. Source: Deck 05, slide 11.

questions.prompt: A running system monitors for an attack and applies a mitigation or patch at runtime. This is an example of what?
questions.correctAnswer: Adaptive mechanisms
questions.explanation: Adaptive mechanisms monitor at runtime and can recover from attacks or patch vulnerabilities at runtime. Source: Deck 05, slide 12.

questions.prompt: In the analysis deck, what is the realization of a threat called?
questions.correctAnswer: An attack
questions.explanation: A threat is a potential event that can compromise a requirement; its realization is an attack. Source: Deck 05, slide 16.

questions.prompt: Which six high-level security engineering tasks are listed?
questions.correctAnswer: architecture,patching,pentesting,requirements,threatmodeling,vv
questions.explanation: The slides list all six as security-focused activities across the development lifecycle. Source: Deck 05, slide 18.

questions.prompt: What is the first step in Microsoft’s six-step application threat-modeling process?
questions.correctAnswer: identify assets
questions.explanation: The first step is to identify the valuable assets the system must protect. Source: Deck 05, slide 36.

questions.prompt: What should an architecture overview document during threat modeling?

choices.label: Subsystems, trust boundaries, and data flow
choices.value: Subsystems, trust boundaries, and data flow

questions.correctAnswer: Subsystems, trust boundaries, and data flow
questions.explanation: The architecture overview uses diagrams/tables for subsystems, trust boundaries, and data flow. Source: Deck 05, slide 37.

questions.prompt: What are the three security-architecture concerns in the slides?
questions.correctAnswer: Protection, detection, and recovery
questions.explanation: Security solutions in the architecture are organized around protection, detection, and recovery. Source: Deck 06, slide 28.

questions.prompt: Which access-control concept belongs to the protection category?

choices.label: Monitoring a manifestation of a threat
choices.value: Monitoring a manifestation of a threat

questions.correctAnswer: Authorization, accountability, and non-repudiation
questions.explanation: The deck places access-control mechanisms under protection and ties them to authorization, accountability, and non-repudiation. Source: Deck 06, slide 31.

questions.prompt: A scanner flags a vulnerability that cannot actually be exploited. What is this?
questions.correctAnswer: False positive
questions.explanation: A false positive is a vulnerability flagged in code that is not exploitable. Source: Deck 06, slide 41.

questions.prompt: Why do static analysis techniques tend to produce false positives?

choices.label: They execute too few test cases
choices.value: They execute too few test cases

questions.correctAnswer: They over-approximate software behavior
questions.explanation: The slides say static analysis tends to over-approximate behavior and therefore tends toward false positives. Source: Deck 06, slide 45.

questions.prompt: Why do dynamic analysis techniques tend to produce false negatives?

choices.label: They do not run the system
choices.value: They do not run the system

questions.correctAnswer: They under-approximate software behavior
questions.explanation: Dynamic analysis observes only executions it exercises, so it under-approximates behavior and tends toward false negatives. Source: Deck 06, slide 47.

questions.prompt: Which penetration-testing approach gives test generation information about design and implementation?
questions.correctAnswer: White-box penetration testing
questions.explanation: White-box testing uses design and implementation information; black-box testing is limited to information essentially available to an attacker. Source: Deck 06, slide 54.

questions.prompt: What does fuzzing do?

choices.label: Feeds public interfaces random, semi-random, and malformed inputs rapidly
choices.value: Feeds public interfaces random, semi-random, and malformed inputs rapidly

questions.correctAnswer: Feeds public interfaces random, semi-random, and malformed inputs rapidly
questions.explanation: Fuzzing rapidly exercises public interfaces with random, semi-random, and malformed inputs. Source: Deck 06, slide 57.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes identification from authentication?

choices.label: Identification uniquely names an entity; authentication proves the asserted identity is genuine
choices.value: Identification uniquely names an entity; authentication proves the asserted identity is genuine

choices.label: Identification grants permissions; authentication revokes them
choices.value: Identification grants permissions; authentication revokes them

choices.label: Identification encrypts data; authentication decrypts it
choices.value: Identification encrypts data; authentication decrypts it

questions.correctAnswer: Identification uniquely names an entity; authentication proves the asserted identity is genuine
questions.explanation: Identification uniquely identifies an entity, while authentication proves the claimed identity. Source: Deck 07, slide 5.

questions.prompt: Why does the deck call user ID plus password the weakest common authentication method?

choices.label: It is single-factor authentication based on something known and is commonly exposed, guessed, or cracked
choices.value: It is single-factor authentication based on something known and is commonly exposed, guessed, or cracked

choices.label: It uses too many independent factors
choices.value: It uses too many independent factors

choices.label: It is based on a private key
choices.value: It is based on a private key

questions.correctAnswer: It is single-factor authentication based on something known and is commonly exposed, guessed, or cracked
questions.explanation: User ID plus password is the common something-you-know single factor and is vulnerable to exposure and guessing/cracking. Source: Deck 07, slide 6.

questions.prompt: What cryptographic model underlies passkeys?
questions.correctAnswer: A public/private key-pair asymmetric cryptosystem
questions.explanation: The slides describe passkeys as based on public/private key-pair asymmetric cryptography and foundational WebAuthn/FIDO technology. Source: Deck 07, slide 8.

questions.prompt: Which are MFA factor categories named in the slides?
questions.correctAnswer: are,have,know
questions.explanation: MFA combines categories such as knowledge, possession/use, and biometrics. Source: Deck 07, slide 10.

questions.prompt: Why are SMS and email one-time passwords considered weaker than some other MFA methods?

choices.label: They can be intercepted or viewed, face device malware/spoofing risks, and need connectivity
choices.value: They can be intercepted or viewed, face device malware/spoofing risks, and need connectivity

choices.label: They require an HSM for every login
choices.value: They require an HSM for every login

questions.correctAnswer: They can be intercepted or viewed, face device malware/spoofing risks, and need connectivity
questions.explanation: The deck notes interception, malware, spoofing/account hijack, and connectivity drawbacks, while still calling them better than password-only SFA. Source: Deck 07, slide 11.

questions.prompt: What does WebAuthn provide in FIDO2?

choices.label: A standard browser/platform web API for FIDO authentication
choices.value: A standard browser/platform web API for FIDO authentication

questions.correctAnswer: A standard browser/platform web API for FIDO authentication
questions.explanation: WebAuthn is the W3C standard web API built into browsers and platforms for FIDO authentication. Source: Deck 07, slide 16.

questions.prompt: How should biometric data be handled according to the slides?

choices.label: Do not transmit/store raw biometrics; generate biometric hashes locally where possible
choices.value: Do not transmit/store raw biometrics; generate biometric hashes locally where possible

choices.label: Store raw biometric recordings in a public database
choices.value: Store raw biometric recordings in a public database

choices.label: Use raw biometrics as a reusable password
choices.value: Use raw biometrics as a reusable password

choices.label: Never account for false positives or negatives
choices.value: Never account for false positives or negatives

questions.correctAnswer: Do not transmit/store raw biometrics; generate biometric hashes locally where possible
questions.explanation: Raw biometrics should not be transmitted/stored; registration generates biometric hashes, ideally in a small local TCB. Source: Deck 07, slide 21.

questions.prompt: In access control, what is a subject?

choices.label: An active entity that interacts with a passive object
choices.value: An active entity that interacts with a passive object

questions.correctAnswer: An active entity that interacts with a passive object
questions.explanation: Subjects are active entities such as users, software, or hardware; objects are passive targets such as files, databases, and devices. Source: Deck 07, slide 27.

questions.prompt: What are privileges in the deck’s terminology?

choices.label: The union of rights and permissions
choices.value: The union of rights and permissions

questions.correctAnswer: The union of rights and permissions
questions.explanation: Permissions grant access on objects and rights allow actions outside permissions; privileges are their union. Source: Deck 07, slide 28.

questions.prompt: Which are the three primary access-control types in the deck?
questions.correctAnswer: corrective,detective,preventative
questions.explanation: Preventative controls stop unauthorized actions, detective controls discover them, and corrective controls return systems to an acceptable state. Source: Deck 07, slide 32.

questions.prompt: Who controls access in discretionary access control (DAC)?

choices.label: The object owner, who can grant, change, or revoke permissions
choices.value: The object owner, who can grant, change, or revoke permissions

questions.correctAnswer: The object owner, who can grant, change, or revoke permissions
questions.explanation: DAC lets object owners control access to users or groups and administer permission changes. Source: Deck 07, slide 36.

questions.prompt: Under mandatory access control (MAC), what must hold for an operation to proceed?

choices.label: The subject clearance must dominate the object sensitivity label
choices.value: The subject clearance must dominate the object sensitivity label

choices.label: The object owner must personally approve every request
choices.value: The object owner must personally approve every request

choices.label: The user must have only one role
choices.value: The user must have only one role

choices.label: The endpoint must be on public Wi-Fi
choices.value: The endpoint must be on public Wi-Fi

questions.correctAnswer: The subject clearance must dominate the object sensitivity label
questions.explanation: MAC uses subject clearance C and object sensitivity L; C must dominate L, with no read-up and no write-down in the stated model. Source: Deck 07, slide 37.

questions.prompt: Which Bell-LaPadula rule protects confidentiality?
questions.correctAnswer: No read-up and no write-down
questions.explanation: Bell-LaPadula’s simple property forbids read-up and its star property forbids write-down to preserve confidentiality. Source: Deck 07, slide 38.

questions.prompt: Which Biba rule protects integrity?
questions.correctAnswer: No read-down and no write-up
questions.explanation: Biba prevents a subject from being corrupted by lower-integrity input (no read-down) and from modifying higher-integrity objects (no write-up). Source: Deck 07, slide 39.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) model address?

choices.label: Conflicts of interest based on a subject’s previous access
choices.value: Conflicts of interest based on a subject’s previous access

questions.correctAnswer: Conflicts of interest based on a subject’s previous access
questions.explanation: Brewer-Nash prevents conflict-of-interest access, using dynamic controls based on prior actions. Source: Deck 07, slide 41.

questions.prompt: What additional inputs can ABAC use beyond subject and object information?

choices.label: Context such as endpoint geolocation, time window, and endpoint health
choices.value: Context such as endpoint geolocation, time window, and endpoint health

questions.correctAnswer: Context such as endpoint geolocation, time window, and endpoint health
questions.explanation: ABAC can apply real-time contextual information and support granular responses such as step-up authentication or reduced access. Source: Deck 07, slide 48.

questions.prompt: What is the semantic distinction between identity management and identity governance in the course slides?

choices.label: Identity management handles accounts, lifecycle, provisioning, roles, and password policy; governance handles access requests/reviews, entitlement creep, SoD, role optimization, and risk analytics
choices.value: Identity management handles accounts, lifecycle, provisioning, roles, and password policy; governance handles access requests/reviews, entitlement creep, SoD, role optimization, and risk analytics

choices.label: They are exactly the same function
choices.value: They are exactly the same function

choices.label: Governance only creates passwords; management only audits access
choices.value: Governance only creates passwords; management only audits access

choices.label: Management is physical access only; governance is encryption only
choices.value: Management is physical access only; governance is encryption only

questions.correctAnswer: Identity management handles accounts, lifecycle, provisioning, roles, and password policy; governance handles access requests/reviews, entitlement creep, SoD, role optimization, and risk analytics
questions.explanation: The deck explicitly contrasts operational identity-management functions with governance functions that prove and review appropriate access. Source: Deck 07, slide 61.

questions.prompt: How do PAM solutions reduce the privileged-identity management problem from P × T toward P + T?

choices.label: Use a hardened credential vault with checkout/in/rotation and hardened logging
choices.value: Use a hardened credential vault with checkout/in/rotation and hardened logging

choices.label: Give every privileged user a shared permanent password
choices.value: Give every privileged user a shared permanent password

choices.label: Store credentials in scripts and stash files
choices.value: Store credentials in scripts and stash files

questions.correctAnswer: Use a hardened credential vault with checkout/in/rotation and hardened logging
questions.explanation: PAM discovers accounts, uses a hardened vault, checks credentials out/in with rotation, and logs actions, reducing the combinatorial credential burden. Source: Deck 07, slide 73.

questions.prompt: Name the three data-security risk-management stages in order: discover, classify, and _____.
questions.correctAnswer: protect
questions.explanation: The slides present the three stages as discover, classify, and protect. Source: Deck 11, slide 14.

questions.prompt: Why is discovery foundational to data protection?

choices.label: Data that cannot be found cannot be protected
choices.value: Data that cannot be found cannot be protected

questions.correctAnswer: Data that cannot be found cannot be protected
questions.explanation: The deck stresses that data is everywhere and says directly: if you cannot find it, you cannot protect it. Source: Deck 11, slide 15.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly relates privacy and confidentiality?

choices.label: You can have confidentiality without privacy, but not privacy without confidentiality
choices.value: You can have confidentiality without privacy, but not privacy without confidentiality

choices.label: Confidentiality is possible only for public data
choices.value: Confidentiality is possible only for public data

questions.correctAnswer: You can have confidentiality without privacy, but not privacy without confidentiality
questions.explanation: The mitigation slide makes this exact distinction. Source: Deck 11, slide 16.

questions.prompt: What security capability must accompany media encryption for it to be dependable at scale?
questions.correctAnswer: Robust, scalable cryptographic key management
questions.explanation: Media encryption relies on robust, scalable cryptographic key management. Source: Deck 11, slide 17.

questions.prompt: Which best describes hardening?

choices.label: Locking down systems with secure configuration, current patches, and disabled unneeded services/functions
choices.value: Locking down systems with secure configuration, current patches, and disabled unneeded services/functions

choices.label: Adding every available service for flexibility
choices.value: Adding every available service for flexibility

questions.correctAnswer: Locking down systems with secure configuration, current patches, and disabled unneeded services/functions
questions.explanation: Hardening uses secure settings, patching, and disables unneeded protocols, services, and functionality. Source: Deck 11, slide 19.

questions.prompt: Which functions can an external database reference monitor provide?

choices.label: Secure logs difficult for DBAs to alter

questions.correctAnswer: discovery,masking,securelog,sqli
questions.explanation: The deck lists these functions alongside SoD controls, alerts, vulnerability scanning, and activity monitoring. Source: Deck 11, slide 21.

questions.prompt: In tokenization, where is the relationship between the original card number and the token stored?

choices.label: In the merchant’s public source code
choices.value: In the merchant’s public source code

questions.correctAnswer: In a separate vault
questions.explanation: The workflow replaces the card number with a token while storing their relationship separately in a vault. Source: Deck 11, slide 24.

questions.prompt: What is DLP intended to detect and prevent?

choices.label: Exfiltration, modification, and/or destruction of important data
choices.value: Exfiltration, modification, and/or destruction of important data

questions.correctAnswer: Exfiltration, modification, and/or destruction of important data
questions.explanation: Data Loss Prevention seeks to detect and prevent loss through exfiltration, modification, or destruction. Source: Deck 11, slide 27.

questions.prompt: Why must restore processes be tested and validated?

choices.label: Backups cannot support recovery if restoration fails when needed
choices.value: Backups cannot support recovery if restoration fails when needed

choices.label: Testing automatically creates a hot standby
choices.value: Testing automatically creates a hot standby

choices.label: Restore testing removes the need for incident response
choices.value: Restore testing removes the need for incident response

questions.correctAnswer: Backups cannot support recovery if restoration fails when needed
questions.explanation: Backups are key to incident response and availability, but the slides warn that restore processes are sometimes not tested or validated. Source: Deck 11, slide 28.

questions.prompt: What is the order of NIST media sanitization levels shown in the deck?
questions.correctAnswer: CLEAR < PURGE < DESTROY
questions.explanation: The slide presents the increasing sanitization scale as CLEAR, then PURGE, then DESTROY. Source: Deck 11, slide 30.

questions.prompt: What should an application do with user-uploaded files before intended use?
